rationale: A concurrent randomised comparison is the only way to separate the display change from next year's order set change. Because the display is a ward setting and prescribers rotate, wards are the unit of randomisation (c2). Reporting follows the CONSORT extension for cluster randomised trials.
alternatives: Prescriber-level randomisation (refused: 40 percent of orders would be exposed to the other arm)
Before-and-after switch (refused: confounded by the order set change)
Stepped-wedge rollout (refused: longer than the vendor contract allows and still confounded by calendar time)
guidelines: CONSORT extension for cluster randomised trials
whyNotMoreComplex: An adverse drug event primary outcome would need many times more wards and years; the trial measures prescriber response with harm as a safeguard.

decision.statement: Pursue a ward-randomised trial of the tiered alert display for six months, stratified by hospital and specialty, with appropriate response to high-severity alerts as the primary outcome and targeted harm surveillance of suppressed moderate interactions, because tiering improved response in a cluster trial (c1), ward randomisation limits contamination (c2), appropriateness is a reliable outcome (c4) and harm surveillance is workable (c3).
decision.question: Should the network run a randomised comparison of tiered and standard alert displays?

criteria.text: Tiering has improved prescriber response in a randomised comparison, and a ward-level design can avoid most contamination.
Suppressed moderate interactions cause more harm than before tiering.

gates.requirement: Vendor confirmation that the tiered display can be enabled per ward
gates.evidence: Vendor note VN-4471 dated 2026-08-12, supplied by the investigator

gates.requirement: Network REB approval of the cluster trial, including the consent approach for prescribers and patients

alternatives: Before-and-after switch to tiering across all wards
Prescriber education on alert types without changing the display
decision.note: Rests on ledger claims c1 to c4; the leads are not cited. The vendor gate is met; the REB has not reviewed the protocol, so the action is blocked.

summary: Ward-randomised trial recommended; the vendor gate is met and the REB gate is unknown.
